```{r}
#| label: setup
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)

table_dir <- file.path("..", "outputs", "tables")
figure_dir <- file.path("..", "outputs", "figures")
```

## Research Question

We use the Total Fertility Rate and the Total Live Births data from the Singapore
Department of Statistics website, hereafter abbreviated as TFR and TLB
respectively. Singapore's TFR has fallen from 5.76 children per woman in 1960
to 0.87 in 2025 — the lowest on record and far below the replacement level of
2.1. Over the same period, TLB declined from 61,775 to 30,004. This sustained
decline is not unique to Singapore: Shair et al. (2024) document a similarly
dramatic fall in Malaysia's TFR from an average of 6.4 infants per woman in 1960
to 1.8 in 2020, and project Chinese and Indian Malaysian fertility rates falling
below 1.0 by 2040.

Understanding which population subgroups drive TFR is essential context for
interpreting these trends. Chen et al. (2018) conduct an elasticity analysis of
Singapore's TFR and find that 20–29-year-old single women and married childless
women aged 30–34 are the most influential groups for changing TFR, yet
Singapore's pro-natalist policies have historically favoured third and
higher-order births — a policy mismatch that limits their effectiveness. The
inability of targeted interventions to reverse the decline motivates a
data-driven time series approach to quantify the trajectory statistically and
produce reliable near-term projections.

**Research question:** How have Singapore's annual TFR and TLB evolved since
1960, and which course-based time series models provide the most reliable
short-term forecasts of each series after residual diagnostic checking?

The question is suited to annual time series methods because both series are
measured once per year over a long observation window (66 years), exhibit
clear trend and autocorrelation structure, and do not contain a seasonal
component that would require higher-frequency data.

## Data

#### Source and Variables

The data are drawn from the Singapore Department of Statistics (SingStat) births
and fertility register, supplied as the file
`data/raw/BirthsAndFertilityRatesAnnual.csv`. The file is in wide format (one
row per demographic series, one column per year); the preparation script
`scripts/01_prepare_data.R` reshapes it into a long-format tsibble indexed by
measure and year.

Two series are retained for analysis:

- **Total Fertility Rate (TFR):** the average number of children a woman would
  bear over her lifetime at the age-specific fertility rates observed in a given
  year. Measured in children per woman.
- **Total Live Births:** the count of live births registered in Singapore in
  each calendar year.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-series-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Analysis series summary"
series_summary <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "series_summary.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(series_summary, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Measure", "First year", "Last year", "N",
                    "First observation", "Latest observation"))
```

#### Data Validation

An automated validation script confirmed: both series present, no missing
observations, no duplicate measure-year keys, years consecutive from 1960 to
2025, and all values strictly positive. No data quality corrections were
required.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-validation
#| tbl-cap: "Data validation checks"
validation_checks <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "data_validation_checks.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(validation_checks)
```

The two series are highly correlated (Pearson *r* = 0.847), confirming that
they move together over the long run while remaining analytically distinct.
All subsequent analyses treat TFR and Total Live Births as separate univariate
time series.

## Exploratory Analysis

#### Level Series

```{r}
#| label: fig-overview
#| fig-cap: "Annual TFR and Total Live Births, Singapore 1960–2025."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "annual_series_overview.png"))
```

Both series decline persistently from 1960 to 2025 (@fig-overview). TFR falls
steeply through the 1960s and early 1970s as Singapore's post-independence
demographic transition accelerated, then levels off near replacement level in
the 1980s and 1990s before resuming a gradual decline. Total Live Births mirrors
this broad pattern, with a notable baby-boom rebound in 1988 (the largest
single-year increase of 9,341 births) followed by continued decline to the
record low of 30,004 in 2025. Neither series is stationary: the mean level
shifts persistently over time.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptive
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics by sub-period"
descriptive <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "transformation_screen.csv"),
                        show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(Measure, period, observations, mean_observed, sd_observed,
         coefficient_of_variation)
kable(descriptive, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Series", "Period", "N", "Mean", "SD", "CV"))
```

The coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean) for TFR declines sharply across the
three 22-year sub-periods (early 1960–1981: CV = 0.41; middle 1982–2003:
CV = 0.10; recent 2004–2025: CV = 0.10), indicating that the large early
variation is not proportional to the mean level. For Total Live Births the CV
is more stable (0.16 → 0.10 → 0.08), consistent with a series where variance
scales more gently with the level.

#### Annual First Differences

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffs
#| fig-cap: "Year-on-year first differences of TFR (top) and Total Live Births (bottom)."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "annual_first_differences.png"))
```

@fig-diffs shows the year-on-year changes. TFR has a mean annual change of
−0.075 (SD 0.146), with the largest single-year decrease of −0.55 in 1967 and
the largest increase of +0.34 in 1988. Total Live Births averages −489 per year
(SD 2,595). The 1988 baby-boom produced the largest single-year increase of
9,341; the sharpest single-year decline of −5,546 occurred in 2001, following
the end of the baby-boom cohort entering peak childbearing age.

The first differences appear considerably more stationary than the level series,
suggesting that one order of differencing will be sufficient for modelling.

## Transformation and Stationarity

#### Scale Selection

```{r}
#| label: fig-scale
#| fig-cap: "Original scale and log-scale standardised series, 1960 = 1."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "scale_comparison.png"))
```

All observations are strictly positive, so logarithmic transformation is
available for both series. @fig-scale overlays original and log-scaled
(indexed) series. For TFR, the CV collapses from 0.41 in the early period to
0.10 in later periods, indicating non-proportional variance; the original scale
is therefore preferred. For Total Live Births, the more stable CV (0.16 → 0.08)
means that log scale could also be used, but the original scale is retained
throughout to maintain comparability between the two series. Log-scale
modelling of live births is noted as an avenue for future model extensions.

#### Autocorrelation Evidence

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stationarity
#| tbl-cap: "Sample ACF1 at the level and after successive differencing"
stationarity <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "stationarity_screen.csv"),
                         show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(Measure, level_acf1, first_difference_acf1, second_difference_acf1)
kable(stationarity, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Series", "Level ACF1", "Diff(1) ACF1", "Diff(2) ACF1"))
```

Table 2 summarises the first-order autocorrelation coefficient (ACF1) at the
level and after successive differencing. Both level series show very high ACF1
(0.915 for TFR, 0.841 for TLB), consistent with non-stationary or near-unit-root
behaviour. Letting $\nabla y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$ denote the first-difference
operator, one order of differencing reduces ACF1 to 0.370 ($\nabla$TFR) and
$-$0.115 ($\nabla$TLB) — values close enough to zero to support approximate
stationarity. Second differencing overshoots, increasing the magnitude of
autocorrelation in both cases ($-$0.401 and $-$0.523 respectively), confirming
over-differencing. These results justify using **d = 1** in all ARIMA candidates.

## Candidate Models

#### Training and Holdout Design

The 66-observation sample is split into a **training window** (1960–2015,
*n* = 56) and a **holdout window** (2016–2025, *n* = 10). All candidate models
are estimated on the training data only. Holdout forecasts are compared to the
observed values to evaluate out-of-sample accuracy.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-forecast-design
#| tbl-cap: "Training and holdout split"
forecast_design <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "forecast_design.csv"),
                            show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(forecast_design)
```

The 10-year holdout represents approximately 15% of the full series, which is
a reasonable proportion for an annual demographic series. A longer holdout would
reduce the training sample and risk underfitting the long-run trend.

#### Model Set

Five candidate models are fitted for each series:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-registry
#| tbl-cap: "Candidate model registry"
model_registry <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "candidate_model_registry.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(model_registry)
```

The two **benchmark** models (Naïve and Drift) provide simple baselines. The
Naïve model forecasts the last observed value; the Drift model adds the average
historical annual change. Any adequately specified model should outperform at
least one of these.

The **linear trend** model (TSLM) tests whether a deterministic regression on a
time index is sufficient to explain the series. Its inclusion is valuable because
it often achieves good holdout accuracy on monotonically declining series, but
the residual structure must be checked carefully.

The **ARIMA** and **ETS** candidates are the two principal course-based
stochastic model families. ARIMA (AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average)
models the differenced series as a linear combination of its own past values and
past innovations; ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonal) uses an exponential smoothing
state-space framework (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, 2021). Orders and parameters
are selected by minimising the corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc;
Hurvich and Tsai, 1989), which penalises model complexity more aggressively than
AIC in small samples.

#### Selected ARIMA Orders

Automatic order selection produced different structures for the two series:

**TFR — ARIMA(0,1,1).** The selected model applies one order of differencing
(*d* = 1) and a single moving-average term (*q* = 1), with no autoregressive
terms (*p* = 0). In the notation of Box et al. (2015), the fitted equation for
$\nabla y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$ is:

$$
\nabla y_t = (1 - 0.799\,B)\,\varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{N}(0,\,0.028)
$$

where $B$ is the backshift operator ($By_t = y_{t-1}$) and $\varepsilon_t$ is
Gaussian white noise with estimated variance $\hat{\sigma}^2 = 0.028$. The
MA(1) coefficient $\hat{\theta}_1 = -0.799$ is highly significant (SE = 0.075,
*t* $\approx$ −10.7, *p* < 0.001). The negative sign means a positive shock in
period *t* is partially reversed in the following period — consistent with
modest short-term mean-reversion in TFR around its declining long-run level.
This ARIMA(0,1,1) is algebraically equivalent to simple exponential smoothing
applied to the first-differenced series, with AICc = −54.80.

**Total Live Births — ARIMA(0,1,0).** Automatic order selection chose a pure
random walk — one order of differencing with no AR or MA terms:

$$
\nabla y_t = \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{N}(0,\,6{,}811{,}530)
$$

No additional parameters improved the AICc (= 1029.14). This specification is
algebraically identical to the Naïve model (point forecast = last observed
value), so the **Drift model** — which augments the random walk with an
estimated constant annual change — provides a more informative alternative:

$$
\nabla y_t = \hat{b} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \hat{b} = -356 \text{ births/year}
$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-terms
#| tbl-cap: "Fitted model coefficients (training sample, 1960–2015)"
model_terms <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "candidate_model_terms.csv"),
                        show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(model_terms, digits = 4)
```

## Model Diagnostics

#### Residual Time Plots

```{r}
#| label: fig-residuals
#| fig-cap: "One-step training residuals by model (columns) and series (rows)."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "candidate_model_residuals.png"))
```

@fig-residuals shows the one-step innovations (residuals) on the training data.
For TFR, the ARIMA(0,1,1) residuals scatter randomly around zero with no
discernible pattern. The linear trend residuals show a pronounced U-shaped
structure — positive in the early period, negative in the middle, then positive
again — confirming that a purely deterministic linear trend fails to capture
the changing rate of TFR decline. For Total Live Births, the ARIMA(0,1,0) and
Naïve models produce identical residuals (as expected for equivalent
specifications); the Drift model residuals are similarly consistent with white
noise.

#### Residual ACF

```{r}
#| label: fig-resid-acf
#| fig-cap: "Residual autocorrelation functions (lags 1–14) for each candidate model."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "candidate_residual_acf.png"))
```

@fig-resid-acf plots the residual autocorrelation functions to lag 14. For TFR,
the ARIMA(0,1,1) residual ACF has no spikes outside the 95% confidence bands,
providing strong visual evidence of adequate fit. The linear trend model leaves
persistent positive autocorrelation at early lags — a clear sign of unmodelled
dynamics. For Total Live Births, the ARIMA(0,1,0), Drift, ETS, and Naïve
residual ACFs are all consistent with white noise; the linear trend again shows
strong autocorrelation.

#### Ljung-Box Tests

The Ljung–Box portmanteau test at lag 10 (Ljung and Box, 1978) provides a
formal check of residual independence. A p-value above 0.05 indicates that
the residuals do not show significant autocorrelation at the 5% level, which
we take as evidence of adequate model fit.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ljung-box
#| tbl-cap: "Ljung-Box residual test (lag = 10) for each candidate model"
ljung_box <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "residual_ljung_box_tests.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
kable(ljung_box, digits = 4,
      col.names = c("Series", "Model", "LB statistic", "p-value"))
```

For TFR, only ARIMA(0,1,1) (p = 0.346) and ETS (p = 0.736) pass the test.
The Naïve and Drift models fail badly (p < 0.001), as does the linear trend
model (LB = 177.5, p < 0.001). For Total Live Births, ARIMA(0,1,0), Drift,
ETS, and Naïve all pass; the linear trend fails decisively (LB = 109.6,
p < 0.001).

## Forecast Evaluation

#### Holdout Accuracy

```{r}
#| label: tbl-holdout-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Holdout forecast accuracy (2016–2025)"
holdout_accuracy <- read_csv(file.path(table_dir, "holdout_forecast_accuracy.csv"),
                             show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(Measure, .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  arrange(Measure, RMSE)
kable(holdout_accuracy, digits = 3)
```

For **TFR** (@tbl-holdout-accuracy), ARIMA(0,1,1) achieves the lowest holdout
RMSE (0.178) and MAE (0.153) of all five candidates. ETS is the closest
competitor (RMSE 0.190). The linear trend extrapolates a long-run trajectory
that substantially overshoots the near-term observed values (MAPE 93%), making
it the weakest performer despite its simple structure.

For **Total Live Births**, the linear trend achieves the lowest holdout RMSE
(2,719) and MAE (2,321). However, its residuals carry severe autocorrelation
(LB = 109.6, p < 0.001), which invalidates its prediction intervals — a model
with correlated residuals will systematically misstate forecast uncertainty.
Among models with adequate residual diagnostics, the **Drift** model achieves
the best RMSE (4,097) and MAE (3,296), substantially better than ARIMA(0,1,0),
ETS, and Naïve (all around RMSE 6,240).

#### Holdout Forecast Plot

```{r}
#| label: fig-holdout
#| fig-cap: "Holdout forecast comparison (2016–2025). Solid black: observed. Shaded: 80% prediction interval."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "holdout_forecast_comparison.png"))
```

@fig-holdout shows the training series, holdout observed values, and 80%
prediction intervals for each candidate. For TFR, the ARIMA(0,1,1) band is
well-centred on the observed holdout path. For Total Live Births, the linear
trend tracks the holdout trajectory closely by extrapolating the long-run
decline, but its prediction intervals are statistically invalid. The Drift
model's intervals are wider but properly calibrated.

#### Model Selection

**TFR — ARIMA(0,1,1) selected.** This model simultaneously achieves the best
holdout RMSE and MAE and passes the Ljung-Box residual test (p = 0.346). No
other candidate improves on both criteria. ETS is retained as a secondary
reference in the forecast figures.

**Total Live Births — Drift model selected.** The linear trend's superior raw
accuracy is disqualified by a catastrophic residual diagnostic failure (LB
statistic = 109.6, p < 0.001): its residuals carry substantial unmodelled
autocorrelation that invalidates any stated prediction interval. Among the four
diagnostically adequate models, Drift achieves the best holdout RMSE (4,097)
and retains an economically interpretable structure — the estimated annual
decline of 356 births per year directly reflects the observed long-run trend.
Although the Drift coefficient for live births is not individually significant
at the 5% level (t = −0.96, p = 0.341), the substantive direction of decline
is supported by over six decades of data and is appropriate for a five-year
projection horizon.

## Final Forecasts

Both selected models are refitted to the full 66-observation series (1960–2025) before producing five-year-ahead forecasts. Using the complete sample rather than the training-only window reduces estimation uncertainty now that model selection is settled.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forecasts
#| fig-cap: "Five-year forecasts (2026–2030) from all candidates refitted to the full 1960–2025 series. Inner band: 80% PI; outer band: 95% PI."
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figure_dir, "five_year_candidate_forecasts.png"))
```

Both selected models are refitted to the complete 66-observation series
(1960–2025) before producing five-year-ahead forecasts (@fig-forecasts). The
selected models — ARIMA(0,1,1) for TFR and Drift for Total Live Births — are
the primary forecasting reference.

**TFR.** The ARIMA(0,1,1) model refitted to 1960–2025 projects a continued
modest decline, with the point forecast for 2030 falling below 0.87. The 95%
prediction interval widens considerably at five years because the
random-walk component accumulates uncertainty each period. The lower bound of
the 95% interval approaches zero by 2030, reflecting substantial statistical
uncertainty at this horizon and underscoring that these projections should be
interpreted as probabilistic rather than precise predictions.

**Total Live Births.** The Drift model projects a continuation of the estimated
annual decline of approximately 356 births per year. The resulting 2030 point
forecast is approximately 28,200, with prediction intervals widening
substantially over the five-year horizon. This forecast is conditional on the
persistence of the average rate of change observed over 1960–2025. Policy
interventions — such as extended parental leave schemes or housing subsidies
for young families — or structural demographic shifts lie outside the model's
assumptions and could alter the trajectory.

**Limitations.** Both final models are purely univariate and include no
demographic covariates. Chen et al. (2018) show that Singapore's pro-natalist
policies have historically targeted third and higher-order births, whereas the
groups most influential for TFR are 20–29-year-old single women and married
childless women aged 30–34; incorporating such subgroup dynamics would require
a richer covariate model. A natural extension within the time series framework
would be to model TLB as a function of TFR — a conditional-forecast approach
demonstrated in the companion analysis — exploiting the Pearson correlation of
0.847 between the two series. The annual data frequency precludes seasonal
decomposition, and the 10-year holdout has limited power to discriminate between
models with similar accuracy. Structural breaks at the sharp 1980s and 2000s
policy shifts are not explicitly modelled.

## Conclusion

This report examined Singapore's annual Total Fertility Rate and Total Live
Births from 1960 to 2025 using time series methods covered in the MATH X313
curriculum. Both series display persistent long-run decline and strong level
autocorrelation (ACF1 ≈ 0.91 and 0.84 respectively), requiring first
differencing before ARIMA estimation.

For TFR, **ARIMA(0,1,1)** was selected on the basis of the best combination of
holdout forecast accuracy (RMSE = 0.178, MAE = 0.153) and clean residual
diagnostics (Ljung-Box p = 0.346). The fitted MA(1) coefficient of −0.799
captures a partial reversion of shocks within one year.

For Total Live Births, the **Drift model** was selected. The linear trend
model's superior raw accuracy was disqualified by a severe violation of the
residual independence assumption (LB = 109.6, p < 0.001), which renders its
prediction intervals statistically invalid. The Drift model passes all
diagnostic checks, captures the long-run declining trend, and achieves the best
holdout RMSE (4,097) among diagnostically adequate candidates.

Five-year forecasts suggest that TFR will continue to decline modestly below
0.87, and total live births will fall toward approximately 28,200 by 2030, with
wide uncertainty bands reflecting the inherent difficulty of demographic
forecasting. Future work should incorporate TFR as a covariate for live-birth
modelling and investigate whether government pro-natalist policy expenditure
constitutes a structural break that improves forecast accuracy.
